The Biscutate swift (Streptoprocne biscutata) is a large, dark neotropical swift that breeds on vertical cliff faces and in rocky canyons across eastern and central South America. As an obligate aerial insectivore, it spends virtually its entire life on the wing, and this extreme lifestyle is reflected in its life-history traits. Field studies of nesting colonies indicate that a single egg represents the typical clutch, though clutches of up to four eggs have been documented in some regions. Females produce approximately 1 to 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 1 to 2 clutches per year], with each clutch containing between one and four eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing between one and four eggs]. This relatively low annual reproductive output is consistent with patterns observed in other large swifts and likely reflects the high energetic costs of foraging over vast distances. During the breeding season, adults maintain high body temperatures around 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], a thermal regime that probably facilitates rapid digestion and assimilation of the small arthropod prey captured during long foraging bouts.

Neonates emerge from the egg after approximately 24 days [ab = approximately 24 days] of incubation at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a developmental period shorter than that of many similarly-sized altricial birds but typical of swifts, which produce relatively small, poorly developed young. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings weigh about 10 grams [Wwb = about 10 grams], placing them at the lower end of the body-mass continuum for hatchling apodiform birds. The newly hatched chick is sparsely covered in down and is entirely dependent on biparental provisioning. Due to the unpredictable nature of aerial insect prey, parents deliver food in the form of a bolus of regurgitated insects, and nestling growth proceeds at a moderate pace. During the incubation period, the female often leaves the eggs unattended for extended periods, relying on the thermal inertia of the nest cavity and ambient conditions to maintain the stable thermal environment required for successful embryogenesis at 36 °C.

The initial wet weight of a freshly laid egg is approximately 11.6 grams [Ww0 = approximately 11.6 grams], with reported values ranging from 10 (10-14.3 grams [Ww0 = 10-14.3 grams]) to 14.3 grams across different clutches and study sites. This represents about 10 to 12 percent of the adult female body mass, a relatively modest investment per egg compared to some other aerial insectivores. The egg is elongated and white, typical of cavity-nesting species, and is laid on a shallow cup of lichen and feathers glued together with saliva. Growth of the nestling is rapid but prolonged by avian standards, with the chick reaching a peak fledging mass that often exceeds adult weight before the characteristic pre-fledging weight loss. Under the thermal conditions characteristic of the active metabolic period, roughly 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], the nestling period lasts approximately 33 days after hatching [tx = approximately 33 days after hatching].

A comprehensive growth study documented that female Biscutate swifts ultimately attain an asymptote in body mass of 119 grams [Wwi = 119 grams], which likely represents the maximum size achievable given aerodynamic constraints and the energetic demands of sustained flight. Males tend to be slightly lighter, though sexual size dimorphism is minimal in this species. The development of flight feathers and the associated increase in locomotor capability proceed gradually, and fledging marks the transition to a life of continuous aerial existence. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal maturation, occurs at approximately 99 days after hatching [tp = approximately 99 days after hatching], though this value shows considerable individual variation, with a reported range of 28 to 39 days i at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]n some studies. This relatively rapid sexual maturation, when viewed in the context of the species' maximum lifespan, suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproduction despite the inherent risks of breeding in challenging cliff-face environments, which are experienced at an active body temperature close to 38.1 °C.

The maximum documented lifespan for Biscutate swift in the wild is approximately 16 years [am = approximately 16 years], a value derived from long-term banding studies of nesting adults at several Braz at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]ilian colonies. This longevity is comparable to that of the closely related common swift (Apus apus), which also exhibits a maximum lifespan of around 20 years. The first successful reproductive event, or age at first brood, typically occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], meaning most individuals do not breed until their second calendar year at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This delayed reproductive onset is common among swifts and other long-lived birds, as it allows young birds to accumulate foraging experience and establish the necessary physiological condition. The reproductive output, sustained at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] during active periods, is complemented by high annual adult survival and an extended reproductive lifespan, which together compensate for the modest yearly clutch production to achieve overall population stability.
